title: In vivo two-photon microscopy protocol for imaging microglial responses and spine elimination at sites of fibrinogen deposition in mouse brain
protocol: Anesthetize the mouse with an intraperitoneal injection of 100 mg ketamine and 15 mg xylazine per kg of body weight, diluted in 0.9% NaCl solution prepared under sterile conditions.
Apply artificial tears ointment to the eyes to prevent dehydration of the cornea.
Shave the head of the mouse.
Disinfect the exposed skin with betadine and 70% ethanol.
Inject 2% lidocaine subcutaneously.
Make an incision of approximately 1 cm to expose the skull.
Thoroughly remove subcutaneous connective tissue.
Clean and dry the exposed skull area.
Make a circular moat of about 3–4 mm in diameter over the somatosensory cortex using a small drill until the bone inside flexes under gentle pressure from a dental micro-scalpel blade.
Attach a custom-designed steel head bar with an imaging chamber to the skull using cyanoacrylate glue and Metabond dental cement.
Apply a drop of pre-warmed (35°C–37°C) ACSF to the imaging chamber over the bone island.
Gently lift off the bone island from the imaging chamber after 1 minute using a dental microscalpel blade as a lever.
Flush the dura mater with pre-warmed ACSF.
Ensure that the imaging chamber is always covered with ACSF to prevent dehydration of the meninges.
Thaw an aliquot of Alexa dye-labeled fibrinogen at 37°C.
Mix the thawed fibrinogen by inverting the tube 2–3 times.
Keep the thawed fibrinogen at 30°C–37°C until ready to inject.
Pre-heat a pulled glass microinjection micropipette to 37°C.
Keep the pre-heated micropipette at 37°C until ready to inject.
If injecting vehicle solution, mix it with a fluorescent dye-labeled dextran.
Inject a small volume of fluorescently labeled dextran diluted in saline intravenously (100 μL, 3%–5% w/v).
Place the mouse on the microscope stage and attach the head bar/imaging chamber to its holder.
Introduce a 25 × or 40 × water-immersion objective lens into the ACSF in the imaging well.
Raise the objective to create room for insertion of the microinjection micropipette underneath the objective.
Back-fill the pre-warmed microinjection glass micropipette with the pre-warmed Alexa dye-labeled fibrinogen solution and insert the micropipette in the injector holder.
Introduce the microinjection micropipette into the ACSF filling the imaging chamber.
Use epifluorescence to locate the micropipette.
Center the micropipette tip into the field of view of the objective lens.
Bring the micropipette tip to focus under epifluorescence guidance.
Gradually lower the injection micropipette with the micromanipulator while simultaneously lowering the objective lens.
Ensure the micropipette tip and objective lens travel the same distance for synchronized movement.
Continue lowering until the dura becomes visible and the micropipette tip is right above it.
Switch to needle insertion mode if available.
Gently insert the micropipette tip through the dura into the top layer of the underlying cortex using the lowest micromanipulator speed settings.
Switch the microscope to 2P laser-scanning mode.
Use the appropriate 2P laser excitation wavelength, dichroic mirrors, and bandpass filters for the Alexa dye-labeled fibrinogen or fluorescent dextran-mixed vehicle/ACSF.
Advance the microinjection micropipette into the cortex until reaching a minimum depth of 70–100 μm below the pial surface.
Set the upper and lower limits of a z-stack so that the tip of the micropipette lies in the middle of the stack.
Start the z-stack acquisition.
Pressure-eject the solution at a pressure of 0.1–0.7 bar and ejection pulse time of 0.5–2 s.
Increase the microinjector’s ejection pulse time to increase the injection volume proportionally.
Confirm successful injection by observing the appearance of a fluorescent cloud around the needle tip.
Set up time-lapse z-stack acquisition parameters using a 1 μm z-step.
Acquire a full z-stack every 2–3 min for a total of 30 min from injection, to evaluate microglial process response to local fibrinogen injection.
Create z-projections of the imaged volumes for each timepoint.
Create a collective timelapse z-stack from all individual z-projections in sequence.
Threshold every image in the timelapse z-stack so that microglial processes have a value of 255 and background is set to 0.
Quantify the number of microglial processes entering from an outer area Y (∼70 μm radius) into an inner area X (∼35 μm radius).
Count the number of white pixels in area X over time (Rx(t)).
Compare Rx(t) with the first picture taken immediately after electrode insertion (Rx(0)).
Calculate the microglial response relative to the number of processes in outer area Y immediately after electrode insertion (Ry(0)).
Determine the microglial response at any time point (R(t)) using R(t) = (Rx(t) – Rx(0)) / Ry(0).
Repeat the same procedure for the control (ACSF) injections.
Plot both responses over time.
Gently flush the craniotomy with ACSF.
Place a round glass coverslip (3 mm in diameter, type 0) on top of the dura.
Seal the edges of the coverslip with Flow-It™ ALC™ composite.
Cure the Flow-It™ ALC™ composite under UV light.
Set an xyz stack of 100 × 100 × 60 μm around the electrode tip.

Inject a small volume (5–10 pL) of the respective solution with a pressure injector at a pressure of 0.35–0.6 bar during simultaneous imaging of neurites, spines, and microglia at 4× optical zoom (40× objective lens).
Acquire additional xyz stacks with the 40× objective lens at 1× and 2× optical zoom.
Acquire additional xyz stacks with the 10× objective lens at 1× optical zoom to create overview maps of the vasculature and dendritic structures for relocation of the same imaging site.
Place and seal a new coverslip over the craniotomy.
Anesthetize the mouse with an intraperitoneal injection of 100 mg ketamine and 15 mg xylazine per kg of body weight, diluted in 0.9% NaCl solution.
Attach the headbar/imaging chamber to the mounting post to fix the mouse underneath the microscope.
Follow the ROI re-location method to re-image the exact same imaging region(s) of interest (ROIs).
Use 10× and 40× vascular overview maps acquired at baseline to re-locate the exact ROI.
Identify the location of fluorescent structures, such as dendrites and dendritic spines.
Quantify long-term effects of microinjected fibrinogen or vehicle on dendrites and dendritic spines for each imaging time point.
Process the 100 × 100 × 60 μm xyz stacks acquired around the glass electrode tip at baseline (day 0/day of micro-injection) and at the same location on day 3 using ImageJ.
Calculate the number of dendrites at day 3 as a percentage of that at baseline/day 0.
Identify dendrites present in both the baseline and day 3 imaging stacks for spine number comparison.
Calculate the number of spines on identified dendrites at day 3 as a percentage of those at baseline.
Quantify changes or equality in spine numbers by researchers blinded to the injection agent.
Administer retro-orbital injection of Alexa dye-conjugated fibrinogen as outlined below at 48 h and 24 h before the imaging experiment.
Thaw the required number of aliquots of Alexa dye-conjugated fibrinogen at 37°C using a heating block.
Invert the solution/aliquot tube 2–3 times after thawing.
Anesthetize the mouse with isoflurane at 1.5%–2% at an oxygen flow rate of 0.5 L/min.
Inject 100 μL of Alexa dye-conjugated fibrinogen retro-orbitally using a 28-gauge insulin syringe.
Insert the syringe into the retro-orbital sinus, located caudally to each eye.
Perform imaging experiments 24 hours after the second injection using the appropriate 2P excitation laser wavelength and emission filter for the Alexa dye-conjugated fibrinogen used.
Put the mouse on a temperature-controlled stereotaxic injection frame.
Fix the head with ear bars.
Fill a Hamilton syringe attached to a beveled 33-G needle with AAV1.hSyn.eGFP.WPRE.bGH (titer ≥ 7×1012 vg/mL).
Move the syringe to the prefrontal cortical area using a dissection scope.
Lower the syringe until the needle tip touches the skull and record the z coordinate.
Repeat steps for measuring the z coordinate of lambda.
Adjust alignment of the mouse head in the stereotaxic device to yield less than 0.3 mm difference between the prefrontal cortical and lambda z coordinates.
Move the syringe to bregma and record A/P and M/L stereotaxic coordinates.
Move the syringe to the somatosensory cortex (in mm from bregma: A/P -0.75, M/L +1.5).
Mark location on the skull.
Raise the syringe.
Drill a hole through the skull at the identified location.
Lower the syringe until the tip of the needle touches the dura mater and record the z coordinate.
Lower the needle to 1.00 mm below the dura mater.
Inject 1 μL of the virus using an autoinjector set at a speed of 60 nL/min.
Wait 5 min for the virus to diffuse.
Slowly raise the syringe.
Perform “Animal surgery” steps 1–13 and “Implantation of chronic glass window for longitudinal in vivo imaging” steps 33–35.
Allow a 14-day incubation time for the virus to infect neurons.
Perform r.o. administration of fluorescently labeled fibrinogen as described under “In vivo fibrinogen labeling: retro-orbital injections of Alexa dye-conjugated fibrinogen” steps 42–44.
On day 2 of the r.o. fibrinogen injection, i.e., one day before imaging, administer Methoxy-XO4 (5 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal injection.
Use screws to secure head bar with the holder, then fix mouse under the 2P microscope.
Use epifluorescence to locate the cranial window.
Locate dendritic spines 100 μm below the dura with and without Alexa 594-labeled fibrinogen deposits and which are located < 50 and > 50 μm of a Methoxy-XO4-labeled amyloid-β (Aβ) plaque.
Use 2P wavelengths of 840 nm and 920 nm and a 40 × objective at 4 × optical zoom.
Acquire a stack of 100 × 100 × 60 μm around the region of interest.
Acquire xyz stacks with the 40 × objective lens at 1 × optical zoom.
Acquire xyz stacks with the 40 × objective lens at 2 × optical zoom.
Acquire xyz stacks with the 10 × objective lens at 1 × optical zoom.
Locate the same imaging area using the 10 × vascular overview map after 14 days.
Locate the same imaging area using the 40 × vascular overview map after 14 days.
Re-image as described in steps 38 and 39.
Unscrew/detach the head bar from its holder and place the mouse back on the heating pad in the surgery area.
Subcutaneously inject 0.5 mL saline as hydration supplement.
Administer analgesic as recommended by veterinary staff and IACUC, e.g., 0.1 mg/kg buprenorphine.
Leave the animal on the heating pad until it has fully recovered from anesthesia.
House the mouse individually.
Provide analgesia every 6–12 h for 2 days post-operatively or as needed, and as recommended by veterinary staff and IACUC.
Daily monitor each mouse to ensure normal behavior and full recovery from each surgical procedure and imaging session.
Do not use anti-inflammatory drugs such as carprofen or dexamethasone before, during, or after surgery for microglia imaging studies.
